newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu urges Syria to stop Lebanon attacks.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu urges Syria to stop Lebanon attacks.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called on Syria to stop Hizbollah guerrilla attacks on Israeli forces in Lebanon after a roadside bomb killed three soldiers on Thursday.
Netanyahu also urged Syria to restart peace talks with Israel suspended for nearly a year.

"We wish peace with Syria and want to resume negotiations with it. But what we are seeing is that Syria, in effect, is enabling an unceasing war against Israel and Israeli soldiers in Lebanon through Hizbollah," he said in a statement released by his office.

"The most simple and basic thing that needs to be done at this moment is for Syria to restrain Hizbollah, stop the war and carnage in Lebanon and of course find with us the formula for returning to the negotiating table," he said.
Three Israeli soldiers were killed and one wounded by a roadside bomb in south Lebanon early on Thursday. Two of the soldiers were buried on Thursday.
Iranian-backed Hizbollah guerrillas claimed responsibility for the attack.

Israel occupies a 15 km (nine mile) wide south Lebanon border strip it patrols with its South Lebanon Army militia allies. Israel contends Syria, the main power broker in Lebanon, could stop Hizbollah attacks if it wanted to.
Thursday's bomb attack raised to four the number of Israeli soldiers killed in Lebanon this year. Last year the toll was 27.
The violence came amid an apparent flurry of diplomatic contacts to restart Israel-Syria peace talks.

European Middle East envoy Miguel Angel Moratinos met Syrian President Hafez al-Assad in Damascus on Wednesday, where he said the Syrians expressed interest in Israeli comments on a formula for restarting negotiations.

The White House said on Wednesday it was preparing to host the leaders of Israel, the Palestinians, Egypt and Jordan in separate meetings with President Bill Clinton over the next two months. One key objective was to restart Israel-Syria talks, a spokesman said.

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said on Thursday he had "no doubt" the sides could find a formula to resume the talks halted by Israel's previous government after a wave of Islamist attacks 11 months ago.
Speaking on Israel's Army Radio, Levy said peace would be good for both countries. "If Syria is interested in peace, peace can serve her to the same extent it can serve us," he said.
"I have no doubt that we can reach a formula that will bridge the stances so Israel will not be the side that folds and the Syrians will not go back to what is called the starting point."

Syria demands Israel resume the talks from the point at which they stopped, insisting the previous Israeli government had approved the principle of full withdrawal from the Golan Heights, seized by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war.

But Netanyahu opposes the land-for-peace formula which has been the basis for five years of negotiations. Israel's previous government said it was willing to make at least a partial return of the Golan.
